# Clarifying ISO 15765-4 and ISO 15765-3 in OBD2 Diagnostics

When working with OBD2 interfaces, it is common to encounter confusion regarding the specific layers of the ISO 15765 stack. The core misunderstanding often stems from conflating the transport layer (ISO 15765-4) with the application layer protocols (ISO 15765-3). While generic OBD2 scanners and tools like ScanTool heavily rely on ISO 15765-4, this choice is not a limitation of the protocol itself, but rather a constraint imposed by the OBD2 specification's definition of "enhanced" diagnostics versus basic compliance.

ISO 15765-4 defines the Upper Layer Services over CAN. Its primary role is to handle data framing and transmission timing. In the context of OBD2, this protocol manages how bytes are sent across the physical bus using either Single Frame or Multi-Fragment transmission. Crucially, ISO 15765-4 is agnostic to the *content* of the message. It simply packages PIDs (Parameter IDs) into frames and waits for a response based on timeouts defined in the OBD2 spec. This is why generic readers work: they implement the transport layer perfectly but only request the mandatory PIDs required by SAE J1979 for basic compliance, such as engine RPM or coolant temperature. They rarely attempt to read extended manufacturer-specific data because they lack the mapping tables and application layer logic to interpret it, even if the bus supports it.

This brings us to ISO 15765-3. This standard defines the "Enhanced Diagnostic" protocol specifically for use with On-Board Diagnostics (OBD) systems. Unlike ISO 15765-4, which is a generic transport mechanism, ISO 15765-3 introduces specific application layer services designed to handle larger payloads and more complex diagnostic sessions without the strict time-out limitations of basic OBD2 requests. It allows for the retrieval of a significantly larger set of vehicle parameters beyond the standard mandated PIDs.

The distinction is architectural. If you are building a tool that needs to read deep into manufacturer-specific data, simply implementing ISO 15765-4 is insufficient if your application logic requires the extended service definitions found in ISO 15765-3. The protocol shift allows for different session states and response handling that standard OBD2 scanners ignore. For instance, ISO 15765-3 supports specific control modes and data page requests that enable reading multi-byte parameters efficiently, whereas basic ISO 15765-4 implementations often struggle with these without falling back to slower, single-byte reads.

Developers looking to implement enhanced diagnostics must be aware that the ECU must explicitly support the ISO 15765-3 application layer. A vehicle might advertise support for extended PIDs over CAN, but if the ECU firmware is configured only for standard OBD2 responses, the application layer negotiation will fail. You cannot assume that enabling the transport protocol automatically unlocks the enhanced data; the ECUs must be flashed or configured with the appropriate diagnostic software stack to recognize ISO 15765-3 requests.

In practice, implementing this usually involves a custom firmware build on the scanner side or utilizing professional-grade diagnostic suites that explicitly map the ISO 15765-3 service definitions. Open-source libraries often default to J1939 or basic J1850/ISO 14229 (UDS) over CAN, which may require a different approach than sticking strictly to the legacy OBD2 ISO 15765 stack if you need full enhanced diagnostics.

If your goal is to build a diagnostic tool that goes beyond fault codes and mandatory parameters, you must ensure your implementation includes the specific application layer logic defined in ISO 15765-3. This often means parsing extended response frames differently than standard OBD2 P0xxx/P1xxx responses. The trade-off here is complexity versus capability: generic tools are cheap and reliable for basic health checks, but they will never give you the deep insights available through the enhanced protocol unless you build a solution capable of negotiating that specific application layer state.
